To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the following two methods can be used to improve the accuracy of a neural network model for the task of few-shot learning: (1) using big prototype tensors instead of small ones, and (2) adding an additional regularization loss term to the training procedure.

(a) we propose a novel prototype learning method that is able to learn more representative prototypes, (b) we demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in the low-data learning scenario, and (c) we show that the proposed method is more effective than state-of-the-art in the few-shot learning scenario.

(1) the prototype vector should be a weighted average over the instance embeddings, where the weights are the class probabilities, (2) the class probabilities are obtained by a simple linear layer, which is trained jointly with the model, and (3) the prototype vector can be a dense vector, i.e., a tensor of arbitrary dimension.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to learn more representative and expressive prototypes for low-data learning.
two questions: (i) How can we represent class-level information in a more expressive way than the mean of instance embeddings?
the following questions: 1. How to construct prototypes that are more representative for each class?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, while there have been some recent attempts to improve the performance of few-shot learning, these methods have been largely limited to specific scenarios and do not generalize well to different datasets and tasks.
the use of dense vectors to represent abstract information has been shown to work well, but there is room for improvement in terms of the expressiveness of the representation.
the use of prototypes in few-shot learning is a promising direction, and there is still much room for improvement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose a new method to learn prototypes that are more representative and expressive for each class, by using a more general form of prototypes, i.e., big prototypes.
we propose to represent prototypes as big tensors, and such tensors can be regarded as ``volumes'' in the feature spaces.
we propose to use a ``dense'' tensor as prototype, which is a weighted average of all instance embeddings.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the expressivity of a prototype is related to the density of the class distribution in the feature space.
we can use big prototypes to represent the whole class-level distribution.
, by increasing the dimension of prototypes, we can represent the class-level information more accurately.
